title: Polycarp to the Philippians
subtitle: an old pastor sends a martyr's letters, and a word against the love of money
lead: Polycarp, the leader of the church at Smyrna in Asia, wrote this letter to the church at Philippi in Macedonia, a church Paul had founded (Acts 16:12-40). The Philippians had welcomed Ignatius of Antioch and other prisoners on their way to die in Rome, and they had written to Polycarp asking for three things: a word of teaching 'about righteousness', a carrier for their letter to the church in Syria, and copies of Ignatius's letters (3:1; 13:1-2). Polycarp answers with a short pastoral letter. He praises their faith (1), teaches each group in the church its duties (4-6), warns against teachers who deny that Christ came in the flesh (7), holds up Christ and the martyrs as examples of endurance (8-9), and grieves over Valens, an elder of Philippi who had fallen through greed (11). With it he sends copies of Ignatius's letters, which the Philippians wanted to collect (13; Lake).

Almost every sentence is made of the words of the New Testament letters, above all 1 Peter, Paul and 1 John, and once, in a line that survives only in Latin, Polycarp calls a passage of Ephesians and the Psalms 'these Scriptures' (12:1). George Reid's article on the canon in the Catholic Encyclopedia counts 'eight of St. Paul's writings' cited in it and calls the testimony of Polycarp and Ignatius 'capital' for Paul's letters. Polycarp's Greek survives only to 9:2 and in chapter 13, which Eusebius quotes; the rest is known from an old Latin translation. No church counts the letter as Scripture. It is in no Bible, though Polycarp himself is honored as a saint and martyr by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches.
facts: No church. It is not among the New Testament books listed by the Council of Trent (Catholic), the Westminster Confession (Reformed), Article VI of the Church of England, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's list of 35 New Testament books, or Athanasius's Festal Letter 39. Jerome says it was still 'read ... in the meetings in Asia' in his day (Lives of Illustrious Men 17).

Polycarp, leader of the church at Smyrna (Eusebius and Jerome call him its bishop), writing with 'the elders with him' (1:0). Irenaeus, who knew him, names the letter as his (Against Heresies 3.3.4). The Catholic Encyclopedia calls it 'one of the best attested documents of antiquity', and notes that 'some extremists, anti-episcopalians in the seventeenth century, and members of the Tübingen School in the nineteenth' rejected it.

Tied to Ignatius's journey to Rome. Jerome says Ignatius 'was put to death the eleventh year of Trajan' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16); P. N. Harrison put his death 'probably towards the end of Trajan's reign, but possibly in the early years of Hadrian', within two or three years of AD 117 (1948). If the letter is one, it was written soon after Ignatius passed through. If it joins two letters (Harrison, 1936), chapter 13 is from that time and chapters 1-12 from 135-137 in Harrison's dating. Polycarp died, 'in all probability', on 23 February 155 (Lake).
Smyrna (modern Izmir, Turkey), writing to Philippi in Macedonia (northern Greece), after prisoners on the road to Rome had passed through both cities.
A pastoral letter in the Greek letter form, which Lake calls a 'covering letter' for the copies of Ignatius's letters sent with it.

Greek. The Greek survives in eight defective manuscripts from one ancestor, all breaking off in 9:2, and in Eusebius's quotations of 9:1-2 and 13:1-2. The rest is known only from an old Latin translation kept with the Latin letters of Ignatius (Lake).
14 chapters: a greeting (1:0) and 37 sections. The Plain English Translation follows Lake's text throughout, with variant entries for the readings in his footnotes.
authorship: It opens 'Polycarp and the elders with him' (1:0) and speaks in Polycarp's voice ('I', 3:1; 11:1; 13:1). It gives Polycarp no title.

Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp, called it 'a very powerful Epistle of Polycarp written to the Philippians' (Against Heresies 3.3.4); in his letter to Florinus he mentions letters Polycarp wrote 'to the neighboring churches' (Eusebius, Church History 5.20.8). Eusebius quotes it twice (3.36.13-15) and notes its use of 1 Peter (4.14.9).

The Catholic Encyclopedia says the letter was rejected by those who wished to discredit the Ignatian letters it supports, and that 'these theories possess no interest now that the genuineness of the Ignatian epistles has practically ceased to be questioned'. Since 1936 the question has been whether it is one letter or two letters by Polycarp later joined (P. N. Harrison; see 'One letter or two?').

audience.to: The church at Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia that Paul had founded (Acts 16:12) and written to, two generations later. It had just welcomed Ignatius and other prisoners in chains (1:1; 9:1), had written to Polycarp with its requests (3:1; 13:1-2), was led by elders and deacons (5:3), cared for widows (4:3), and was troubled by the fall of one of its elders, Valens, with his wife (11:1-4).
audience.why: To answer the Philippians' requests, and above all to steady a church shaken by a leader's greed. Polycarp warns every group against the love of money, reminds them of the gospel and of the resurrection and judgment, guards them against false teaching, and tells them not to treat the fallen elder as an enemy but to call him back. Knowing that the letter leads up to the case of Valens changes how its long code of duties reads: it is pastoral care for a church in a crisis, not a general manual.
views: Written in one piece soon after Ignatius passed through Philippi, with the copies of his letters attached (Lake's introduction; the Catholic Encyclopedia).

A short covering note (chapter 13) sent while Ignatius was still on the road, and a later 'Crisis Letter' (chapters 1-12) about Valens, joined in one text (P. N. Harrison, 1936, and his reply of 1948).

outline: Greeting from Polycarp and the elders
Joy over the prisoners and the Philippians' faith; saved by grace
Serve the risen Judge; the Lord's words on judging and mercy
Why Polycarp writes; Paul's wisdom and letters; faith, hope and love
Love of money; wives and widows
Against those who deny the flesh, the cross and the resurrection
Hold to Christ and imitate his endurance
The example of Ignatius, Zosimus, Rufus and Paul
Firm faith, love and alms (from here in Latin)
'Be angry, but do not sin'; prayer and blessing
Letters for Syria; the letters of Ignatius

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a historical source: Polycarp and his date, the link with Ignatius's journey, whether chapters 9 and 13 show one letter or two, and the state of the text (Greek to 9:2, Eusebius for 9 and 13, Latin for the rest).

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Follows the New Testament in the letter: which books Polycarp uses (1 Peter, Paul's letters including 1 and 2 Timothy, 1 John, sayings close to Matthew and Luke), how he introduces them, and what that shows about the books read in Asia in his time.

lenses.name: Church life and the churches
lenses.desc: Reads the letter for what it shows of a second-century church: elders, deacons, widows, virgins, discipline of a fallen elder, almsgiving, prayer for rulers, the collecting of a martyr's letters, and how today's churches remember Polycarp.

sections.b: The Plain English Translation is made from Kirsopp Lake's Greek text (Loeb, 1912) where the Greek survives (1:0-9:2 and 13:1-2), and from the old Latin translation that Lake prints for 10:1-12:3, the last sentence of 13:2 and 14:1. In the Latin chapters the English is a translation of a translation, and the notes say so. Quotations of the New Testament are given in the site's own wording of the verse where Polycarp's Greek matches it, and translated as he gives them where he adapts them; the notes mark each one. Key terms follow the rest of the site: 'elder' for presbyteros, 'deacon' for diakonos, 'love of money' for philargyria, 'resident alien' in the greeting (1:0).

Lake: Polycarp 'was the Bishop of Smyrna in the first half of the second century, and was martyred, in all probability, on February 23rd, 155', at eighty-six; he 'had been a disciple of John, and opinions differ as to whether this John was the son of Zebedee, or John the Presbyter'. Irenaeus, who heard him as a boy, says apostles appointed him in Smyrna, that he visited Rome under Anicetus, and that he called Marcion 'the first-born of Satan' (Against Heresies 3.3.4). The story of his death is told in the Martyrdom of Polycarp, also on this site.

sections.h: The occasion: Ignatius and his letters
sections.b: Ignatius, overseer of Antioch, was taken under guard through Asia to Rome. He wrote four letters from Smyrna and three from Troas, one of them to Polycarp (Eusebius, Church History 3.36.3-10), and in them he asked the churches to send messengers and letters to Antioch, whose church was now at peace (To Polycarp 7-8; To the Smyrnaeans 11). From Troas he sailed to Neapolis, the port of Philippi (To Polycarp 8). The Philippians welcomed him and his companions, then wrote to Polycarp asking him to forward their letter to Syria and to send them what letters of Ignatius he had (13:1-2). Lake: Polycarp's letter is, 'as we should say, a "covering letter"' for those copies, and it is 'interesting to notice that the one epistle which neither Polycarp nor the Philippians could easily obtain would be that to the Romans', the one whose manuscripts have 'a different textual history from that of the other six'.

sections.h: The New Testament in the letter
sections.b: Lake's margin prints about fifty references to Scripture for these 37 sections, nearly all to the New Testament. Polycarp draws most on 1 Peter (1:3; 2:1-2; 7:2; 8:1-2; 10:2), which Eusebius noticed (Church History 4.14.9); on Paul, whom he names (3:2; 9:1; 11:2-3), including Ephesians (1:3; 12:1), Philippians (5:2; 9:2; 12:3), 1 Corinthians (5:3; 11:2), Galatians (3:3; 5:1) and 1 and 2 Timothy (4:1; 5:2; 9:2; 11:4; 12:3); on 1 John and 2 John (7:1); and on sayings of Jesus close to Matthew and Luke (2:3; 7:2). He introduces Jesus' words as 'what the Lord said' (2:3; 7:2), Paul's as 'as Paul teaches' (11:2), and in 12:1 calls the lines of Ephesians 4:26 and Psalm 4 'these Scriptures'. The Catholic Encyclopedia quotes Lightfoot: 'sentence after sentence is frequently made up of passages from the Evangelical and Apostolic writings'.

sections.h: The Greek, Eusebius and the Latin
sections.b: Lake: the letter 'is preserved in eight defective Greek MSS., representing a single archetype, in two long quotations in Eusebius, and in a Latin version contained in the Latin version of the Corpus Ignatianum'. The Greek manuscripts all stop in 9:2 (Lake's footnote: 'Here G breaks off, but the rest of the sentence is given by L Eus.'). Eusebius quotes 9:1-2 and 13:1-2 (Church History 3.36.13-15), so for chapter 13 his quotation is the only Greek, and it stops before the last sentence. For 10-12 and 14 the Latin is the only witness. Lake: 'A full collation of the individual Greek and Latin MSS. is given by Lightfoot.'

In 9:1-2 Ignatius is already 'with the Lord'; in 13:2 Polycarp asks for news of 'Ignatius himself and those who are with him'. P. N. Harrison (Polycarp's Two Epistles to the Philippians, 1936) explained this by two letters: an early 'Covering Note' (chapter 13), written while Ignatius was still on the road, and a later 'Crisis Letter' (chapters 1-12) about Valens and the false teachers, which he dated about 135-137 and took as aimed at Marcion. In his reply of 1948 he names C. J. Cadoux and C. H. Dodd as agreeing 'that Polycarp wrote two letters, one before, the other after, the death of Ignatius', while contending that the second came 'only a few months, or at most a year or two, after the first' and denying 'any reference to Marcion'; and Carl Schneider (1937) as accepting the theory 'in both its parts'. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1911) holds to one letter: Polycarp 'wrote his epistle before he had heard of St. Ignatius' martyrdom', so 9:2 counts the condemned Ignatius among the martyrs while 13:2 asks for firm news. Lake (1912) treats the letter as one 'covering letter'. The chapter pages for 9 and 13 give both sides.

Read it as a letter to a hurting church. The opening praise (1) and the reminder of the gospel (2) prepare for the duties of each group (4-6), which in turn prepare for the one case Polycarp names, the elder Valens and his wife (11). Read it with Paul's Philippians open, since Polycarp writes to the same church in its own words, and with 1 Peter, whose language he uses most. And read it beside the Martyrdom of Polycarp: the man who writes 'let us imitate his endurance' (8:2) later died for the same faith.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the code is built around the fallen elder
spec.body: This is Claude's own reading. The duties in 4:2-6:3 grow longer as they go, and the longest are the elders' (6:1). Every quality Polycarp asks of the elders answers what went wrong with Valens: 'far from all love of money', 'not quick to believe a charge', 'not harsh when they judge', 'knowing that we all owe a debt of sin'. The warnings against greed for widows and deacons (4:3; 5:2) make the point general before it becomes personal. And Polycarp's silence about any overseer at Philippi may be tact: in a church whose leadership had just failed, he speaks of 'the elders and deacons' as a body (5:3) rather than of one office-holder. Harrison's name for chapters 1-12, the 'Crisis Letter' (1936), points the same way.

prompts: Prisoners on the road to Philippi (1:1; 9:1)

On a Roman road through low hills toward a walled hill-town with a theater and columns, a small group of believers in plain tunics walks beside three chained prisoners, one an older bearded man (Ignatius) whose wrist chains glint like a royal band; Roman soldiers march ahead and behind; a woman offers bread, a man carries a bundle of scrolls; dust and evening light.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

In a small upper room in Smyrna, an old white-bearded man sits at a low wooden table writing on a papyrus sheet with a reed pen; beside him lie rolled copies of letters tied with cord, a clay lamp, and an ink pot; two other elders stand nearby, one holding a rolled letter sealed for travel; through a window, a harbor with a merchant ship.

canon.summary: Polycarp to the Philippians is an early Christian letter in no church's Bible. Its author, the martyr Polycarp, is honored as a saint by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches.
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books (1546) does not include it. The U.S. bishops' liturgical calendar keeps 23 February as the day of 'Saint Polycarp, Bishop and Martyr'. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls the letter 'one of the best attested documents of antiquity'.

Not part of the Bible: Reid (1908) states that the Eastern Orthodox churches 'have a New Testament identical with the Catholic'. The Orthodox Church in America commemorates 'Hieromartyr Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna' on 23 February, and its life of him speaks of the letter as his only surviving epistle, which, it says, Jerome testifies was read 'in the churches of Asia Minor at divine services'.

Not in their New Testaments as Reid (1908) describes them: he names the extra books of the Armenian New Testament ('one apocryphal letter to the Corinthians and two from the same') and of the Coptic-Arabic Church ('the Apostolic Constitutions and the Clementine Epistles'), and says the Syrian 'Monophysites receive all the book'; Polycarp's letter is not among the additions.
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books, which includes the 27 and eight further books, among them 'The book of Clement' and the 'Didascalia', does not name it.

Not Scripture: Article VI receives 'all the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'. The Church of England's Common Worship calendar lists '23 Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna, Martyr, c.155' in February.
Commemorates 'Polycarp of Smyrna, Pastor and Martyr' on 23 February and says he was 'executed for his faith on February 23, c. 156', a year later than Lake's date.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament and holds that Scripture is 'all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these'.
Not Scripture: the Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 New Testament books, 'all of which are given by the inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life'.

provenance.h: Smyrna, in the generation after the apostles
provenance.b: Polycarp wrote from Smyrna, in Asia, to Philippi, in answer to a letter from the Philippians, after Ignatius had passed through both cities in chains (1:1; 9:1; 13:1-2). Lake treats it as a covering letter for the copies of Ignatius's letters sent with it. The date depends on the date of Ignatius and on whether chapters 13-14 and 1-12 were written at the same time (see the book sections).

Eight Greek manuscripts from one ancestor, all breaking off in 9:2; Eusebius's quotations of 9:1-2 and 13:1-2; and a Latin version kept with the Latin letters of Ignatius (Lake). Irenaeus knew the letter and wrote of it while Eleutherius was bishop of Rome (Against Heresies 3.3.3-4).

rejected_why.h: It never claims to be apostolic
rejected_why.b: The early church received as New Testament the writings it held to come from the apostles and their circle. Polycarp writes as a later teacher who sets himself far below Paul: 'neither I nor anyone like me is able to follow the wisdom of blessed and glorious Paul' (3:2). He sends the Philippians back to Paul's letters and quotes the apostles' writings as authorities over his own.

No ancient list of the New Testament includes it. Eusebius's survey of accepted, disputed and rejected books (Church History 3.25) does not mention it, though he quotes the letter elsewhere (3.36.13-15). Athanasius's Festal Letter 39 (367) names the 27 books and, besides them, books 'appointed by the Fathers to be read' by new believers, such as the Teaching of the Apostles and the Shepherd; Polycarp's letter is not among them. Jerome says it was 'read to the present day in the meetings in Asia' (Lives of Illustrious Men 17), as a valued letter rather than a book of the canon.

cited_in.b: The risen Christ's letter to the church at Smyrna, Polycarp's own church, promises 'the crown of life' to those faithful to death. Polycarp's letter does not quote it, but it speaks of chains as the 'crowns' of the chosen (1:1).
Paul greeted the Philippians 'with overseers and deacons'; Polycarp, writing to the same church, names its 'elders and deacons' (5:3) and no overseer.
A 'Crescens' went to Galatia; Polycarp's letter carrier is Crescens (14:1). The name was common, and nothing in either text links the two men.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what Christians in Asia and Macedonia believed and did in the early second century, the letter is of the first importance: Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp, names it as his, the Catholic Encyclopedia calls it 'one of the best attested documents of antiquity', it is early, and it shows a church that already read 1 Peter, Paul's letters and 1 John as its authorities. As a text it is weaker than most of the New Testament: the Greek is lost for a third of it, and the Latin there is the only witness. Its few historical statements fit what Ignatius's letters and Eusebius say. Its teaching agrees closely with the New Testament, which it quotes far more than it adds to.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to early Christian faith and life
sections.b: Very high. The letter is early (Polycarp died in 155, Lake), its author knew people who had known the apostles (Irenaeus), and its picture of church life, elders and deacons, widows who pray, care for the poor, discipline of a fallen leader, prayer for rulers, matches Ignatius's letters (To the Smyrnaeans 8; 13). Its heavy use of New Testament books is evidence of which books were read and how they were cited.

Mixed. For 1:0-9:2 the Greek rests on eight late manuscripts from one ancestor, checked in two places by Eusebius. For 13:1-2 Eusebius's quotation is the only Greek. For 10:1-12:3, the last sentence of 13:2 and 14:1, only the Latin version survives, so the exact Greek wording there cannot be known; the Latin manuscripts differ in small points (variants at 11:1, 11:3 and 12:2).

The letter makes few, and they fit the other evidence: Ignatius's journey through Philippi and his request for messengers to Syria (Ignatius, To Polycarp 7-8; To the Smyrnaeans 11), and Polycarp's collection of his letters (Eusebius, Church History 3.36). The tension between 9:2 and 13:2 about whether Ignatius had died is real and is explained in two ways (one letter or two). Nothing in the letter is miraculous.

Matches: salvation 'by grace ... not from works' (1:3, Ephesians 2:8-9); Christ's real flesh, cross and resurrection (7:1, 1 John 4:2-3); the coming judgment (2:1; 6:2); love of enemies and prayer for rulers (12:3). Goes beyond: widows as 'God's altar' (4:3), an image the New Testament does not use; the saying 'alms rescue from death' (10:2), from Tobit. Points the churches read differently: Tobit is in the Council of Trent's Old Testament; Article VI of the Church of England reads it 'for example of life and instruction of manners' but not 'to establish any doctrine'; the Westminster Confession counts it 'no part of the canon of Scripture'. A reader who takes Ephesians 2:8-9 as the rule may find 10:2 in tension with it, and the condition in 2:2, 'if we do his will', raises the same question. The site's cards at Proverbs 16 and Tobit 4 (giving and forgiveness) and at Ephesians 2, Romans 3 and James 2 (faith and works) set out each church's reading.

how_to_read.h: As a letter, not a treatise
how_to_read.b: Polycarp answers a particular church with a particular trouble, the fall of an elder through greed (11). Read the whole letter with that case in mind.
Most of Polycarp's sentences are made from the apostles' words. Following the notes back to 1 Peter, Philippians, Ephesians, 1 Timothy and 1 John shows both what he received and how he used it.
The writer who urges the Philippians to imitate Christ's endurance (8:2) and honors the martyrs (9:1-2) was himself burned at Smyrna. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, on this site, tells that story.
